extracted.intended_audience: university technology-transfer professionals, university administrators, and legal counsel advising academic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on copyright ownership, transfer, enforcement, defenses, and special rules as applied to university-created works and technology-transfer contexts. Covers termination, works-for-hire, registration, infringement (direct and indirect), fair use, educational exceptions, and doctrines limiting copyright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination rights under the 1976 Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Author or author’s heirs may terminate a transfer, license, or grant of copyright approximately thirty-five years from publication or forty years from the license/transfer; the right is nonassignable and termination cannot be waived in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Termination exists because of unequal bargaining power; works for hire are excluded; termination allows creators or successors to renegotiate and share in unexpected success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works for hire exclusion from termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Works made for hire are explicitly excluded from the termination provision of the Copyright Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory definition of works for hire is narrowly construed to protect creators; parties may not simply designate a work as 'for hire' to avoid termination protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment-created works and rebuttal of presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials created in the course of employment are presumed works for hire unless rebutted by a written agreement signed by both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unilateral policy manuals or unsigned policies are insufficient; obtain signed agreements to change statutory presumption (cases involving photographs and faculty works discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly-work tradition (faculty ownership)
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities have traditionally not claimed copyrights in scholarly works; courts have recognized faculty ownership of academic articles and scholarly works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserting university ownership of scholarly works can raise difficult legal and political issues; many institutions leave scholarly copyright with faculty subject to limited exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint authorship standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint work is prepared by two or more authors with the intention that contributions be merged into inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole; each joint author is a co-owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Goldstein’s test, a contribution must be original expression that could stand on its own; courts consider creative control, objective manifestations of intent to be co-authors, and audience appeal. Co-ownership claims have a three-year statute of limitations; each joint author may exploit the work but may owe accounting for profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written requirement for transfers (assignment/ownership)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any transfer of copyright ownership must be in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a transfer agreement that omits the word 'copyright' satisfies the writing requirement is a matter of interpretation; best practice is explicit, signed written assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive license treated as ownership transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive license is treated as a transfer of ownership; the owner of an exclusive license can bring an infringement action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exclusive licensee generally cannot transfer rights without the licensor's consent; licensors retain rights not specifically granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing requirement limited to exclusive licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing requirement of the Copyright Act applies only to exclusive licenses; nonexclusive licenses may be oral or implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonexclusive licenses can arise from conduct; however, to avoid uncertainty, express written licenses or assignments are recommended where ownership/control is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied licenses are narrowly found
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have found implied licenses only in narrow circumstances—e.g., where one party created a work at another's request and delivered it intending the other to copy and distribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting on the Internet does not necessarily create an implied license for commercial use (Microstar v. Formgen example). The limited case law does not support broad implied licenses for commercial exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to obtain express written assignments from contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure ownership, the safest course is to require an express written assignment from all persons working on material expected to be owned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express assignments eliminate uncertainty about ownership and rights to exploit the work, though termination rights may still arise decades later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration required before suit and confers benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration (for works created since Jan 1, 1978) is not mandatory but is required before commencing a copyright infringement action and allows recovery of statutory damages and attorney fees if infringement is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expedited registration may allow statutory damages for infringements that commenced before registration; include accurate disclosures of preexisting works, author identity, and creation/publication dates to avoid fraud claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of inaccurate registration statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration inaccuracies can lead to claims of fraud on the Copyright Office, but registrations are generally not invalidated absent intent to conceal material facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: file accurate applications to minimize litigation attacks based on registration defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity for registrations within five years
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration within five years of publication creates a presumption of ownership and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special caution for software owners who submit massive source code collections without identifying original portions—presumption may be weakened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative classification of works
rubrics_metrics.description: The Copyright Act sets forth eight categories of works; the Register of Copyrights may allocate works to administrative classes by regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative classification has no effect on subject matter or exclusive rights; erroneous classification in registration should not invalidate registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie elements of copyright infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement a plaintiff must prove (1) ownership of a valid copyright and (2) copying of protected expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership is often established by registration; copying can be inferred by circumstantial evidence of access and substantial similarity. Independent creation is a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation or authorization of violation of any exclusive statutory rights without permission of the copyright owner constitutes infringement; direct infringement does not require intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection extends beyond literal text to nonliteral elements of expression (plot, characters, sequence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of nonliteral elements and substantial similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protection extends to unauthorized paraphrasing that uses nonliteral elements; courts consider unique setting, characters, plot, and sequence of events as protectable expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction between idea and expression is critical—ideas are not protected; only expression that is original and concrete may be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apple analytic dissection test for infringement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-step approach: identify sources of alleged similarity; analytically dissect to determine which similar features are protected expression (separating unprotectable ideas); define the scope of the plaintiff's copyright and then apply a subjective comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic dissection may use expert testimony and a list of criteria of comparison; after dissection, jurors may subjectively compare based on the defined scope of protection. This approach narrows protection in some software/audiovisual contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of comparison for analytic dissection
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic dissection examines concrete elements such as plot, themes, dialogue, mood, setting, pace, sequence of events, and characters to determine protectable features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria help separate idea from expression and identify what aspects deserve protection; if most similarities derive from ideas, only near-identical copying supports infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and arrangement and thin copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright can extend to the selection and arrangement of unprotected components; such a compilation may receive 'thin' protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where works largely consist of unprotectable elements, infringement is unlikely absent 'bodily appropriation' or virtual identity; thin protection limits scope of exclusive rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement: vicarious and contributory liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties not directly infringing may be liable under vicarious or contributory infringement doctrines depending on their role, control, knowledge, and financial interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different tests apply for vicarious vs contributory liability; cases involving BBS, Napster, and Grokster illustrate how technology and control affect liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicarious liability test
rubrics_metrics.description: Vicarious liability arises if a defendant has the right and ability to supervise the infringer and a direct financial interest in the infringement, even without actual knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may impose liability where a facilitator profits and has supervisory authority over infringing activity (e.g., trade show organizer renting booths and charging admission).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement test
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may be liable for contributory infringement if in a position to control use of the copyrighted work and knowingly induces, causes, or materially contributes to unauthorized use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulletin board operators have been held liable in some cases; mere hyperlinking has been held not to constitute contributory infringement in some precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service-provider liability and technology-specific analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability of service providers depends on knowledge of infringement, ability to block or supervise users, and the technology's architecture (centralized index vs decentralized networks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napster was held liable due to knowledge and ability to block; Grokster was (at time of writing) distinguished by decentralized architecture and lack of actual control. The Supreme Court later established an inducement standard (liability for purposeful, culpable expression or conduct that fosters infringement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal liability for willful infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1992, felony penalties may apply where the infringer acts willfully and for commercial advantage or private financial gain; penalties include imprisonment up to five years and fines up to $250,000 when certain thresholds are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threshold example: within a six-month period copying at least ten works with retail value > $2,500; the NET Act expanded prosecutable conduct by removing the commercial-gain requirement in certain contexts (e.g., BBS operators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary remedies (damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: For infringement after registration, the owner can recover statutory damages (up to $150,000 per work for willful infringement) and attorney fees; for any infringement, actual damages (owner's loss or infringer's gain) are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration timing affects availability of statutory damages and fees; choose registration strategy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign immunity defense
rubrics_metrics.description: States and state institutions may be immune from federal copyright suits under the Eleventh Amendment unless they have consented to be sued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress’s attempt to abrogate such immunity (Copyright Remedy Clarification Act) was found to exceed its power; thus, suits against states require consent or waiver of immunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use statutory factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Four statutory factors determine fair use: (1) purpose and character of use (including commercial vs nonprofit and transformative nature), (2) nature of the copyrighted work, (3) amount and substantiality used, and (4) effect on the market for the copyrighted work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformative uses weigh in favor of fair use. Case examples: Sony/Connectix (intermediate copying for reverse engineering found fair use), Kelly v. Arriba (search-engine thumbnails fair use for indexing), Ticketmaster (data extraction may be fair use), Texaco (unauthorized photocopying by corporate users weighed against fair use). Availability of reasonable licensing alternatives cuts against fair use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom copying guidelines (brevity, spontaneity, cumulative effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-binding legislative-history guidelines allow limited classroom copying: single copies for personal use or class preparation; multiple copies for classroom use must include copyright notice and meet brevity, spontaneity, and cumulative-effect tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity = short portions; spontaneity = teacher's immediate need preventing permission-seeking; cumulative effect = limited repeated use (e.g., not more than nine times per term from same course) and not directed by higher authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEACH Act rules for distance learning
rubrics_metrics.description: TEACH permits mediated instructional activities by accredited nonprofit educational institutions under conditions: the use is an integral part of class experience, controlled/supervised by instructor, comparable in amount/type to live classroom, technological measures limit transmission to enrolled students and prevent retention, and copyright policies/information provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TEACH does not permit creating individual copies for students, and it does not apply to works produced/marketed primarily for digital transmission (e.g., many textbooks or course packs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Library and archive reproduction (section 108) and 'rule of five'
rubrics_metrics.description: Libraries and archives have limited reproduction rights under 17 U.S.C. §108; legislative-history 'rule of five' permits a single entity to receive up to five articles published in the last five years from the same periodical in any year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Libraries must post the prescribed copyright warning (37 C.F.R. §201.14) and follow statutory limits for reproduction and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-sale doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The first-sale doctrine distinguishes copyright from the physical copy: once a copy is lawfully sold, the copyright owner’s control over that physical copy is exhausted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software is often licensed rather than sold and therefore may not be subject to the first-sale doctrine; licensing terms can prevent downstream resale or transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public domain and preexisting materials
rubrics_metrics.description: When a copyright owner’s exclusive rights are extinguished the work enters the public domain; copyright does not protect portions incorporating preexisting works in the public domain or owned by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shareware is not necessarily public domain; open-source models use contract plus copyright to ensure continued control and to prevent works from entering the public domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merger doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of a work that must necessarily be used as incident to an idea, process, or system are not copyrightable; where idea and expression are inseparable (merged), only identical copying is barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merger frequently limits protection for software functionality or formats where there are only a limited number of ways to express the idea (examples: table formats, matrix displays for extracting characters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes à faire doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression dictated by external factors, stereotyped expression, or standard/common features necessary for a given subject matter are excluded from copyright protection absent virtual identicality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes à faire and merger are closely related; both bar protection for expression that is essentially the only or standard way to express an idea or to achieve compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of operation exclusion for software
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional aspects of software—procedures, processes, systems, or methods of operation—are not eligible for copyright protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held user-interface structures like menu command hierarchies (Lotus menu tree) can be uncopyrightable as methods of operation even if words/structure are similar, limiting protection for software implementations.
